questionText: What is a production subsidy, and who pays for it?
answers: A payment from domestic producers to the government, funded by taxpayers
A tax on imported goods, collected by the government from foreign producers
A payment from the government to domestic producers, funded by taxpayers
A payment from consumers to domestic producers to boost their revenue
explanation: A production subsidy is a payment from the government to domestic producers, funded by taxpayers. Note the direction of the money and who ultimately bears it: it is not paid by consumers, and it is not collected from foreigners — a tax on imports would be a tariff.

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: The diagram shows the domestic market for solar panels, which trades at the world price of $200 per panel. What quantity of panels is imported?
explanation: At the world price of $200 domestic firms supply 20,000 panels while consumers demand 80,000. Imports fill the gap: 80,000 − 20,000 = 60,000 panels.

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: At the world price of $200, how many panels are made by domestic producers?
explanation: Read across from the world price of $200 to the SUPPLY curve: domestic firms are willing to make 20,000 panels at that price. The rest of what consumers want is imported.

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: The government introduces a $200 subsidy per panel paid to domestic producers. By how much does domestic production rise?
explanation: The subsidy shifts the domestic supply curve down by $200 — producers now need only $200 from the market to cover a panel that used to need $400. Domestic output rises from 20,000 to 40,000 panels: an increase of 20,000.

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: With the $200 subsidy in place, by how much do imports fall?
explanation: The subsidy does not change the world price, so consumers still buy 80,000 panels — demand is untouched. Domestic production rises from 20,000 to 40,000, and every extra panel made at home is one not imported, so imports fall by 20,000 (from 60,000 to 40,000).

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: How much does the $200 subsidy cost the government?
explanation: The government pays the subsidy on every panel made domestically, not just the extra ones: $200 × 40,000 panels = $8 million. Multiply by the NEW domestic quantity, not by the increase.

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: After the $200 subsidy, what price do domestic buyers now pay per panel?
explanation: Nothing has happened to the world price. Panels can still be imported at $200, so domestic sellers cannot charge more than that — buyers still pay $200. A production subsidy raises output, not the price consumers face.

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: After the subsidy, what price do domestic producers effectively receive per panel?
explanation: Producers receive the $200 the buyer pays PLUS the $200 subsidy from the government = $400 per panel. That gap between what the buyer pays and what the producer receives is the whole point of the subsidy.

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: Starting from free trade, what size subsidy per panel would be needed to reduce imports to 20,000?
explanation: Demand stays at 80,000, so imports of 20,000 means domestic production must reach 60,000 panels. Domestic firms only supply 60,000 when they receive $600 a panel. Buyers still pay the world price of $200, so the subsidy must fill the gap: $600 − $200 = $400.

title: Market for solar panels
questionText: Starting from free trade, what size subsidy per panel would be needed to eliminate imports entirely?
explanation: To remove imports entirely, domestic production must cover all 80,000 panels demanded. Domestic firms supply 80,000 only at $800 per panel. Buyers still pay $200, so the subsidy must be $800 − $200 = $600.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: This is the domestic market for bicycles, which trade at the world price of $100 per bike. What quantity of bikes is imported?
explanation: At the world price of $100 domestic firms supply 20,000 bikes while consumers demand 80,000. Imports fill the gap: 80,000 − 20,000 = 60,000 bikes.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: At the world price of $100, how many bikes are made by domestic producers?
explanation: Read across from the world price of $100 to the supply curve: domestic firms make 20,000 bikes at that price.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: The government introduces a large $200 subsidy per bike paid to domestic producers. By how much does domestic production rise?
explanation: This subsidy is large relative to the $100 world price, so the supply curve shifts a long way. Domestic output rises from 20,000 to 60,000 bikes — an increase of 40,000.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: With the $200 subsidy in place, by how much do imports fall?
explanation: Demand is unchanged at 80,000 bikes because buyers still pay the world price. Domestic production rises from 20,000 to 60,000, so imports are squeezed from 60,000 down to 20,000 — a fall of 40,000, exactly matching the rise in domestic output.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: How much does the $200 subsidy cost the government?
explanation: The subsidy is paid on every bike made domestically: $200 × 60,000 bikes = $12 million. Note this is far more than the $6 million consumers spend on those bikes — the taxpayer is contributing more than the buyer.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: After the subsidy, what price do domestic producers effectively receive per bike?
explanation: Producers get the $100 the buyer pays plus the $200 subsidy = $300 per bike. Buyers pay $100, because the world price has not moved.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: How much do domestic consumers spend on domestically-produced bikes (valued at the price they pay)?
explanation: Consumers pay the world price of $100 and buy 60,000 domestically-made bikes: $100 × 60,000 = $6 million. Value it at the price the buyer actually pays, not the price the producer ends up receiving.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: Adding the government subsidy to that consumer spending, what is the total revenue received by domestic bike producers?
explanation: Domestic producers receive money from two sources: $6 million from consumers plus $12 million from the government = $18 million. You can check it directly: 60,000 bikes × $300 received per bike = $18 million.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: Starting from free trade, what size subsidy per bike would be needed to reduce imports to 40,000?
explanation: Demand stays at 80,000, so imports of 40,000 means domestic production must reach 40,000 bikes. Domestic firms supply 40,000 when they receive $200 a bike. Buyers still pay $100, so the subsidy is $200 − $100 = $100.

title: Market for bicycles
questionText: Starting from free trade, what size subsidy per bike would be needed to eliminate imports entirely?
explanation: To wipe out imports, domestic production must cover the full 80,000 bikes demanded. Domestic firms supply 80,000 only at $400 a bike. Buyers still pay $100, so the subsidy must be $400 − $100 = $300.
